reason: The six-word run is an artifact of two independent boilerplate strings meeting at a clause boundary — 'unto this people' ends one sentence and 'and thou hast not' begins the next. Exodus 33:12 is Moses complaining that God has not told him whom he will send; Helaman 10:4 is God commending Nephi for not fearing men. Nothing else of Exodus 33 is present, and the window is blind to the fact that it spans a full stop.

The machine's top-ranked source for the phrase is the messianic judge of Isaiah 11:4, who smites the earth 'with the rod of his mouth'. It should not be taken. “smite the earth” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, and only one of them — Revelation 11:6 — also contains 'have power over', which Helaman 10:6 has immediately before it and in the same order. The link is written at Revelation 11:6, where the rest of the grant (shutting heaven against rain) is spent in Helaman 11. Malachi 4:6, the third instance, is a curse on the land at the end of the prophets and has no other contact here.

A genuine five-word match and the senses are opposed. In Jeremiah 38:15 the prophet refuses to speak — 'If I declare it unto thee, wilt thou not surely put me to death?' — and the clause is the protasis of a refusal made by a man in a dungeon to the king who put him there. In Helaman 10:6 God declares to Nephi, in the presence of angels, a grant of power. The same five words face in opposite directions, and there is an ironic near-miss worth naming: Helaman 10:15 has the crowd trying to put Nephi in prison, which is where Jeremiah is speaking from. It is a coincidence of narrative furniture, not a borrowing.

“in the presence of mine” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, which is why it ranked, and the singleton is real but empty: Psalm 23:5's noun is 'enemies' and Helaman 10:6's is 'angels', and everything the phrase shares is the preposition and the possessive. Nothing else of Psalm 23 is anywhere in the chapter. The possible Lukan source of the phrase (Luke 15:10) is recorded as a low-confidence link at the verse.

A temptation worth naming because the chapter has just been talking about a temple. “the Lord God Almighty” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — Revelation 21:22, 'I saw no temple therein: for the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are the temple of it' — three verses after Helaman 10:8 gave Nephi power to rend a temple in twain, which is a pairing a careful reader would want. It will not bear the weight. The determiner is what makes Revelation 21:22 a singleton, and the shorter 'Lord God Almighty' occurs in five KJV verses, all in Revelation (4:8, 11:17, 15:3, 16:7, 21:22). Helaman 10:11 does not have even that: it has 'the Lord God, who is the Almighty', a relative-clause periphrasis matching no KJV verse. The commonplace was available to any nineteenth-century writer without Revelation 21.

reason: “had spoken these words unto” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and the singleton is worthless, exactly as CONVENTIONS §9 says of this same verse — Job 42:7 was the pilot's standing example of rare boilerplate outranking real links. The construction is a speech-closing formula ('when X had spoken these words unto Y') that the KJV writes a dozen ways and the Book of Mormon writes constantly; the rarity measures the KJV's preference for 'when he had thus spoken', not any relation between Job and Nephi. Job's clause introduces God's rebuke of Eliphaz; Helaman's introduces a prophet turning back toward a crowd.

The window closes one word early, in the way ADJUDICATING §4 warns about: Luke 4:29's next word is 'down headlong' off a cliff, Helaman 10:15's is 'into prison'. But the machine is pointing at the right episode for the wrong reason, and the register should say so. Luke 4:29-30 is the Nazareth crowd that tries to destroy the prophet and out of whose midst he passes untouched, which is precisely Helaman 10:15-16 — and the link for that is written at 10:16, on John 5:13's 'conveyed' and Acts 8:39-40's Spirit-borne removal, where the verbal evidence actually is. Luke 4:30 is recorded there as a composite.

The five words agree and the object does not: Luke 20:26's verb is 'take hold of his words' — the spies fail to catch Jesus in speech — while Helaman 10:16's is 'take him', a failed physical arrest. The scene the Book of Mormon is actually running here is the failed arrest of John 7:44-46 (opened at 10:1) and the escape of John 5:13, both catalogued. Luke 20:26 shares a negated auxiliary and a very common verb.

Refusal-to-hearken is one of the Book of Mormon's most-used formulas and one of the KJV's; the phrase appears in Helaman 10:13, 10:15 and 10:18 alone. Covered by the standing exclusion for connective matches (CONVENTIONS §5); recorded once here because Ezekiel 20:8 was ranked, and passed over in silence at its other occurrences.
